english: on the tip of my tongue
also: it was on the tip of my tongue
at the tip of my tongue
I can’t think of the word
I can’t think of the name

terms.gloss: be on the tip of one’s tongue
terms.grammar: prīmōrēs, prīmōrum, the front part, with labrum, labrī n., lip
evidence: Plaut. Trin. 4.2.65: versābātur mihi in labrīs prīmōribus (Lewis & Short s.v. prīmōris)
terms.comment: Latin keeps the word on the front of the lips, not the tip of the tongue. Prīmōribus labrīs attingere is something else: to touch a subject lightly (Cic. de Or. 1.87).

terms.gloss: come to mind, occur to one: nōn succurrit, it won’t come to me
terms.grammar: the word or name is the subject, the person in the dative: nōmen mihi nōn succurrit
evidence: Sen. Ep. 3.1: sī nōmen nōn succurrit
Cic. Att. 14.1.2: ut enim quidque succurrit, libet scrībere
Lewis & Short s.v. succurrō: “to come into the mind, occur to one (class.; esp. freq. after the Aug. period)”
terms.comment: The plain prose way to say that a word or a name will not come: Seneca speaks of greeting people as domine when their name does not come to mind.

phrases.english: It was on the tip of my tongue.

phrases.latin: Dēvorāvī nōmen imprūdēns modo. … Atque etiam modo vorsābātur mī in labrīs prīmōribus.
phrases.english: I’ve swallowed the name without meaning to, just now. … And it was on the tip of my tongue a moment ago.

phrases.latin: quōmodo obviōs, sī nōmen nōn succurrit, «dominōs» salūtāmus
phrases.english: as we greet people we meet as “sir” when their name doesn’t come to mind

phrases.latin: nōmen quidem scrīptōris statim dīximus, rem, dē quā scrīptum fuit, dictūrī haesimus
phrases.english: we told him the author’s name at once, but when we came to say what the book was about, we were stuck for the word

phrases.latin: Excidit mihi verbum; quid dīcimus, cum pluit et sōl lūcet?
phrases.english: The word has gone out of my head; what do we say when it rains and the sun is shining?

sources: Lewis & Short: primoris · Lewis & Short: succurro
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 109.
